rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin joins the hamza of istabraq and declines it; al-Ālūsī suggests irregular hamza deletion or an Arabic derivation from glittering cloth.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن محيصن ( واستبرق ) بوصل الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes regard istabraq as Arabic, despite earlier reports to the contrary; the discrepancy may reflect two readings, declinable and indeclinable.
rows.anchor: وأكثر التفاسير على أنه عربي وليس بمستعرب

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinnī calls the reading with fatḥa on qāf a slip; Abū Ḥayyān replies that it can be a past-tense verb, so it need not be a slip.
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن جني أن قراءة فتح القاف سهو أو كالسهو

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān argues the form can be parsed as a past-tense verb, so the reading need not be a slip.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان : وإنما قال ذلك لأن جعله اسما ومنعه من الصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pairing silk with brocade signals that Paradise offers what its people desire, with fabrics beyond worldly examples and imagination.
rows.anchor: وفي الجمع بين السندس والإستبرق إشعار ما بأن لأولئك القوم في الجنة ما يشتهون

rows.speaker: أبو الخير مرفد بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū al-Khayr reports that a tree in Paradise grows the silk used for its inhabitants’ clothes.
rows.anchor: أخرج البيهقي عن أبي الخير مرفد بن عبدالله قال : في الجنة شجرة

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet said Paradise’s garments split forth from its fruits, rather than being worn or woven beforehand.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر قال : قال رجل يا رسول الله أخبرنا عن ثياب أهل الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adornment precedes clothing because jewelry is more cherished, valuable, and pleasing; passive adornment implies servants perform it, while clothing is attributed actively because people put it on.
rows.anchor: وقدمت التحلية على اللباس لأن الحلي في النفس أعظم وإلى القلب أحب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal that passive adornment means divine favor and active clothing means earned entitlement has a Muʿtazilī implication, which al-Ālūsī says can be answered.
rows.anchor: وقيل : بني الاول للمفعول والثاني للفاعل إشارة إلى أن التحلية تفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arāʾik is the plural of arīka, a bed within a canopy; without the canopy it is not called an arīka.
rows.anchor: ( جمع أريكة كما قال غير واحد وهو السرير في الحجلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās defines an arīka as a bed within a canopy.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ذلك البيهقي عن ابن عباس وقال الراغب

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib derives arīka either from the arāk tree used in ground structures or from a word meaning settled residence.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب : الأريكة حجلة على سرير وتسميتها بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active attribution of clothing fits that people put on garments themselves, especially those covering nakedness.
rows.anchor: وأسند اللبس إليهم لأن الإنسان يتعاطى ذلك بنفسه خصوصا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj defines arāʾik as furnishings in canopies; Abū al-Jawzī reports a sense of couches in Abyssinian.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج : الأرائك الفرش في الحجال والظاهر

rows.speaker: أبو الجوزي
rows.claim: Abū al-Jawzī says in Funūn al-afnān that arāʾik means couches in Abyssinian.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو الجوزي في فنون الأفنان أنها السرر بالحبشية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reclining on couches signifies luxurious comfort and ease; reports also describe sustained enjoyment.
rows.anchor: كناية عن تنعمهم وترفههم فإن الاتكاء على الأرائك شأن المتنعمين

rows.speaker: الهيثم بن مالك الطائي
rows.claim: Al-Haytham reports the Prophet saying a man may recline forty years without moving or tiring, as every desired pleasure is brought to him.
rows.anchor: عن الهيثم بن مالك الطائي أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال إن الرجل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that couches in Paradise have layered bedding extending a farsakh in the sky.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر وجماعة عن ابن عباس أن على الأرائك فرشا

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin shifts the hamza’s vowel to the article’s lām, assimilates the lām, and deletes the alif in ʿalā arāʾik.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن ( علرائك ) بنقل حركة الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet’s contracted ʿal-arḍ means ʿalā al-arḍ, supporting the reading.
rows.anchor: ومثله قول الشاعر : + فما أصبحت علرض نفسي برية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Niʿma al-thawāb means promised Paradise and bliss; ḥasunat may describe the couches or gardens, with murtafaq a reclining place.
rows.anchor: نعم الثواب ( ذلك الذي وعدوا به من الجنة ونعيمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The example addresses believers who worship morning and evening and unbelievers demanding their expulsion.
rows.anchor: ( واضرب لهم ( للمؤمنين الذين يدعون ربهم بالغداة والعشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two objects are the two men, with the second needing exposition; they may be hypothetical, but al-Ālūsī favors historicity.
rows.anchor: مفعولان لا ضرب ثانيهما أولهما لأنه المحتاج إلى التفصيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One account identifies Israelite brothers: the unbeliever Fartūs or Quṭfayr and the believer Judah.
rows.anchor: فقيل هما أخوان من بني إسرائيل أحدهما كافر اسمه فرطوس وقيل اسمه قطفير والآخر مؤمن اسمه يهوذا في قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil names the believer Yamlīkhā.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : اسمه يمليخا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another account makes them sons of an Israelite king: one spent wealth for God, while the other disbelieved and pursued worldly adornment.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنهما ابنا ملك من بني إسرائيل أنفق أحدهما ماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A narrative says they were blacksmiths or inherited and divided eight thousand dinars; the believer spent his share seeking heavenly gardens, a home, spouses, and immortal youths, then became needy and was rejected by his brother.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهما كانا حدادين كسبا مالا وروي أنهما ورثا من أبيهما ثماني آلاف دينار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A different identification makes them Banū Makhzūm: al-Aswad ibn al-Asad and Abū Salama ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Asad.
rows.anchor: وقيل هما أخوان من بني مخزوم كافر هو الأسود بن الأسد والمؤمن هو أبو سلمة عبدالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable contrasts disobedience amid divine favors with obedience amid poverty, rather than repeating the previously described afterlife outcomes.
rows.anchor: بل من حيث عصيان الكفرة مع تقلبهم في نعم الله تعالى وطاعة المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gardens’ location is unspecified because identifying it adds no significant benefit.
rows.anchor: لم يتعين سبحانه مكانهما إذ لا يتعلق بتعيينه كبير فائدة

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن القاسم الكاتب
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Qāsim’s Wonders of Lands says Lake Tinnīs was the site of the gardens, divided by God in one night.
rows.anchor: وذكر إبراهيم بن القاسم الكاتب في كتابه عجائب البلاد أن بحيرة تينس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A garden of grapes means vineyards, either by implied addition or figuratively; al-Rāghib says the word can denote fruit and vine.
rows.anchor: من أعناب ( من كروم متنوعة فالكلام على ما قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Palms surrounded and framed the vineyards; the bāʾ supplies a second object, and crops between the gardens joined staple foods with fruits.
rows.anchor: وحففناهما بنخل ( أي جعلنا النخل محيطة بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basrans treat kiltā as singular in form but dual in meaning; Baghdadis treat it as dual in both form and meaning.
rows.anchor: و ( كلتا ) اسم مفرد اللفظ مثنى المعنى عند البصريين

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh derives tāʾ from wāw and the alif as feminine, raising an inflection problem; al-Jarmī instead treats the alif as original, a proposal al-Ālūsī rejects.
rows.anchor: وتاؤه منقلبة عن واو عند سيبويه فاصلة كلوى فالألف فيه للتأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun with kiltā may follow its singular form or dual meaning; the verse follows form here and meaning later.
rows.anchor: وعلى المشهور يجوز في ضميره مراعاة لفظه ومراعاة معناه وقد روعي الأول هنا

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh’s codex has masculine kulla with ātā because garden is grammatically feminine, but not naturally so.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف عبد الله ( كلا الجنتين آتى ) بصيغة التذكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gardens yielded mature fruit without any decrease, unlike orchards whose harvests vary by year or tree.
rows.anchor: أي لم تنقص من أكلها

rows.speaker: يحيى بن أبي عمرو الشيباني
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿAmr identifies the river as Abū Firṭus, a well-known river in al-Ramla according to Ibn Abī Ḥātim.
rows.anchor: قال يحيى بن أبي عمرو الشيباني : وهذا النهر هو المسمى بنهر أبي فرطس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative that each garden had its own river is contrary to the apparent singular.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى فجرنا فيما بين كل من الجنتين نهرا على حدة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains intensive fajjarnā by the river’s length, as though it were multiple rivers.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : لأن النهر ممتد فكأنه أنهار

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash, Sallām, Yaʿqūb, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read the verb lightly, its basic form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش وسلام ويعقوب وعيسى بن عمر ( فجرنا ) بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: أبو السمال
rows.claim: Abū al-Sammāl and others read nahr with a still hāʾ, a dialectal form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السمال والعياض بن غزوان وطلحة بن سليمان ( نهرا ) بسكون الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning fruit before the river suggests each independently completes the gardens’ beauty and hints that fruit can grow without irrigation, as in 24:35.
rows.anchor: وفيه إيماء إلى أن إيتاء الأكل لا يتوقف على السقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamar means kinds of wealth, not tree produce, which does not fit the passage.
rows.anchor: ثمر ( أنواع المال كما في القاموس وغيره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The reading thumur denotes abundant wealth such as gold, silver, and livestock; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda explain it so.
rows.anchor: وبذلك فسره ابن عباس وقتادة وغيرهما

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid restricts thumur to gold and silver.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد يراد به الذهب والفضة خاصة

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash, Abū Rajāʾ, and Abū ʿAmr read thumur with still mīm; Abū Rajāʾ also has a fatḥa-and-sukūn variant, with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش وأبو رجاء وأبو عمرو بضم الثاء وإسكان الميم

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s codex has the explanatory phrase wa-ātaynāhu thamanan kathīran, We gave him abundant wealth.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أبي وحمل على التفسير ( وآتيناه ثمرا كثيرا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His companion is the believer; the lexical sense of companion does not rule out the men being brothers. Yuḥāwiruhu denotes reciprocal speech.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالصاحب المعنى اللغوي فلا ينافي هذا العنوان القول بأنهما كانا أخوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafar means attendants and helpers, or male children according to Qatāda and Muqātil, or the man’s clan.
rows.anchor: حشما وأعوانا وقيل : أولادا ذكورا وروي ذلك عن قتادة ومقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālan and nafaran are accusative specifications; the comparative apparently has its literal sense, conflicting with reports that the believer remained destitute after giving away his wealth.
rows.anchor: ونصب ( مالا ونفرا ) على التمييز وهو على ما قيل محول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes the singular garden collectively as all the man’s enjoyments, implying this is his only garden and he has no share in the promised Garden.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب الزمخشري وهو معنى لطيف دق تصوره على أبي حيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī finds the collective singular subtle and supported by context: he entered the garden with his companion.
rows.anchor: والذي يدل عليه السياق والمحاورة أن المراد ودخل جنته مع صاحبه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says one walled orchard divided by a river counted as two gardens; al-Ālūsī calls this unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن السدي أنه قال في قوله تعالى ( جعلنا لأحدهما جنتين )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being unjust to himself is circumstantial: disbelief exposes him to ruin and his blessings to loss, or he misplaces what should have been gratitude and humility.
rows.anchor: وهو ضار لنفسه بكفره حيث عرضها للهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speech starts as an answer to the question prompted by his entering the garden in an unjust state.
rows.anchor: قال ( استئناف مبني على سؤال نشأ من ذكر دخول جنته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabīda means perish; his garden would last for his life, not literally forever. Cosmic readings are rejected as strained.
rows.anchor: أي تهلك وتفنى ويقال بادبيد بيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāʾima, literally standing, is a conventional metaphor for the Resurrection’s future occurrence and realization.
rows.anchor: وما أظن الساعة قائمة ( أي كائنة فيما سيأتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He imagines that after resurrection he will receive a better garden, presumptuously treating worldly favor as proof of inherent merit; this is istidrāj.
rows.anchor: ومقدار هذا الطمع واليمين الفاجرة اعتقاد أنه تعالى إنما أولاه ما أولاه

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr and other readers recite the dual pronoun minhumā, referring to both gardens, unlike min-hā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن الزبير وزيد بن علي وأبو بحرية وأبو جعفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording echoes 41:50; rudadtu here reflects painful separation from his cherished garden, while a later passage uses rajaʿtu without that attachment.
rows.anchor: وهذا كقوله تعالى حكاية ( ولئن رجعت إلى ربي إن لي عنده للحسنى )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dialogue framing is an independent circumstantial clause that signals the ensuing exchange is carefully presented as conversation.
rows.anchor: جملة حالية كالسابقة وفائدتها التنبيه من أول الأمر على أن ما يتلوها

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s explanatory reading replaces yuḥāwiruhu with yukhāṣimuhu, he was disputing with him.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي وحمل ذلك على التفسير ( وهو يخاصمه )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbeliever was created from soil through Adam, whose constitution contained humankind’s pattern, so the attribution is real through his origin.
rows.anchor: أي في ضمن خلق أصلك منه وهو آدم عليه السلام لما أن خلق كل فرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation traces his material to soil because male fluid develops from food whose sources return to soil, a figurative attribution from cause to effect.
rows.anchor: وقيل خلقك منه لأنه أصل مادتك إذ ماء الرجل يتولد من أغذية راجعة إلى التراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says an angel puts soil into each sperm destined to become human; al-Ālūsī recalls possible authentication but notes problems applying it here.
rows.anchor: ونقل أنه ما من نطفة قدر الله تعالى أن يخلق منها بشرا إلا وملك موكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sperm is the nearer material origin; one person is made from successive origins. Taswiya means proportioning and perfecting in a balanced form.
rows.anchor: هي مادتك القريبة فالمخلوق واحد والمبدأ متعدد

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān parses rajulan as a circumstantial accusative; al-Ḥawfī instead takes it as a second object and stresses God made him male.
rows.anchor: على ما قال أبو حيان على الحال وهو محوج إلى التأويل

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī parses rajulan as the second object of sawwā, emphasizing that God made him a man.
rows.anchor: وقال الحوفي : نصب على أنه مفعول ثان لسوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charge of disbelief answers doubt about resurrection, entailing doubt about God’s power, truthfulness, and wisdom; linked to 23:115.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى إلى قوله عز وجل ( أفحسبتم أنما خلقناكم عبثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other commentators take him to have been an idolater; akafarta then means did you associate partners, since acknowledging a Lord does not exclude idolatry.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : الظاهر إنه كان مشركا كما يدل عليه قول صاحبه

rows.speaker: ثابت البناني
rows.claim: Thābit al-Bunānī reads waylaka akafarta, adding woe to you as an explanatory reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ثابت البناني وحمل ذلك على التفسير

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: The contracted lakinna-huwa is explained as lakin anā; Ubayy and al-Ḥasan read the full form, also attributed to Ibn Masʿūd.
rows.anchor: أصله لكن أنا وقد قرأ به أبي والحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One derivation shifts the hamza vowel to nūn, then deletes hamza and its vowel and assimilates the nūns; simple deletion and assimilation is closer but irregular.
rows.anchor: فنقل حركة همزة أنا إلى نون لكن فحذفت الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line with lakin iyyāki lā uqlī shows the contraction can mean lakin anā lā uqlīki; other reconstructions are less plausible.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء الحذف والإدغام في قوله : وترمينني بالطرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hāshimī’s transmission from Abū Jaʿfar drops the final alif in connection and pause, a reading also reported from Abū ʿAbla and others.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية الهاشمي عن أبي جعفر حذفها وصلا ووقفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lakin is a non-governing contrast particle; the main parsing makes anā the subject and huwa a pronoun of the matter, with alternatives discussed.
rows.anchor: و ( لكن ) في جميع هذه القراءات حرف استدراك لاعمل له وأنا مبتدأ أول

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī allows nā as a first-person plural pronoun of majesty with rabbi singular by sense; al-Ālūsī considers it remote.
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو علي كون نا ضمير الجماعة كالتي في خرجنا وضربنا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya proposes lakin governs an omitted noun, but al-Ālūsī objects that this requires a reading he did not know.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية في الآية : يجوز أن تكون لكن هي العاملة

rows.speaker: عيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī reads lakin with a still nūn, also attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḥasan.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى الثقفي ( لكن هو الله ) بسكون نون لكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast means you disbelieve, but I believe and affirm God; lā ushriku adds monotheism, while shirk can mean disbelief generally.
rows.anchor: وملخص المعنى لمكان الاستفهام الذي هو للتقرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some explain the companion’s shirk literally: denying resurrection attributes inability to God and equates the Creator with creatures.
rows.anchor: وقيل الشرك فيه بالمعنى المتبادر وإثباته لصاحبه تعريضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says worldly vanity and inherent entitlement amount to implicit association; al-Ālūsī judges both strained.
rows.anchor: وقيل باعتبار أنه لما اغتر بدنياه وزعم الاستحقاق الذاتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī calls both explanations strained; another view sees indirect praise of the believer’s distinction.
rows.anchor: والإنصاف أن كلا من القولين تكلف وقيل في الكلام تعريض بشرف صاحبه

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت عميس
rows.claim: Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays reports the Prophet taught her words for distress: God is my Lord, and I associate nothing with Him.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن أسماء بنت عميس قالت : علمني رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer’s hope may be the conditional answer, or the whole sentence may answer; Kathīr reads it as expecting God to reverse their fortunes.
rows.anchor: قائم مقام جواب الشرط أي إن ترن كذلك فلا بأس

rows.speaker: كثير
rows.claim: Kathīr says the believer expects a better garden through faith while God strips the unbeliever’s blessings for disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقال كثير : هو جواب الشرط والمعنى إن ترني أفقر منك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some restrict the better garden to the afterlife; another allows this life or the next, and the immediate threat suggests worldly consequence.
rows.anchor: وقيد بعضهم هذا الايتاء بقوله : في الآخرة وقال ءاخر : في الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains ḥusbān as punishment, and elsewhere defines it as fire.
rows.anchor: كما أخرجه ابن جرير عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: نافع بن الأزرق
rows.claim: In a question from Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq, Ibn ʿAbbās says ḥusbān means fire.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الطستي عنه أن نافع بن الأزرق قال له : أخبرني

rows.speaker: حسان
rows.claim: Ḥassān’s verse uses ḥusbān for a shower of meteors descending on a people.
rows.anchor: وأنشد له قول حسان : بقية معشر صبت عليهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk also explains ḥusbān as punishment in reports from Ibn Abī Shayba and Ibn Abī Ḥātim.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ذلك ابن أبي شيبة وابن أبي حاتم عن الضحاك أيضا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī derives ḥusbān from calculation or estimation and takes it as a destructive decree; al-Zajjāj supplies punishment, but al-Ālūsī says no omitted noun is needed.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري : هو مصدر كالبطلان والغفران بمعنى الحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī also gives ḥusbān as projectiles such as thunderbolts; other views include hail, stones, or any missiles of punishment.
rows.anchor: ونقل الزمخشري أن ( حسبانا ) جمع حسبانة وهي المرماة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan explains ṣaʿīdan zalaqan as land without vegetation, also transmitted from al-Suddī.
rows.anchor: ليس فيها نبات قاله الحسن وأخرجه ابن أبي حاتم عن السدي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the land becomes shifting, terrifying sand; Abū Ḥayyān apparently prefers literal slippery ground without plants or firm footing.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : أي فتصبح رملا هائلا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān apparently prefers the literal slippery surface, stripped of vegetation and secure footing.
rows.anchor: وظاهر صنيع أبي حيان اختياره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāʾiran means water sunk into the earth; the verbal noun intensifies the sense.
rows.anchor: أي غائرا في الأرض والتعبير بالمصدر للمبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one could seek the sunken water, meaning it is inaccessible; denying ability to seek it signals recovery is impossible.
rows.anchor: فلن تستطيع له ( أي للماء الغائر ( طلبا

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Māwardī takes the pronoun to mean replacement water, rather than the specific sunken water; al-Ālūsī says this is contrary to the apparent reading.
rows.anchor: وقيل ضمير ( له ) للماء مطلقا لا للماء المخصوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If coordinated with become barren, ḥusbān must mean divine judgment causing both outcomes; if coordinated with send, any proposed sense can work.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه ( يصبح ) عطف على ( تصبح )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordination with send permits a heavenly or earthly disaster including water sinking, though one might expect an explicit verb making the water sink.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون العطف على ( يرسل ) وحينئذ يجوز أن يراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars see the conditional phrase as answering the owner’s boast; it answers wealth partly, and fewer or more children may imply lower or higher status.
rows.anchor: ثم أن أكثر العلماء على أن قوله ( إن ترن ) الخ في مقابلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possible reasons for not wishing harm to the children include avoiding harm to innocents or enough reproof through garden loss; another view says children are implicitly included in khayran.
rows.anchor: وكان الظاهر أن يتعرض في الجزاء لأمر الولد كما تعرض لأمر المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says a better garden implicitly includes better children; al-Ālūsī says garden superiority naturally concerns trees, fruit, and water.
rows.anchor: وقيل : أراد ما هو الظاهر أي جنة خيرا من جنتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others say he omitted children because he already had enough or because the afterlife lacks procreation; al-Ālūsī questions these explanations.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لم يترج الولد اكتفاءا بما عنده منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposal says offspring were not paired with the hoped-for garden because the afterlife is not a place of procreation; al-Ālūsī finds this unconvincing.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه لم يقرن ترجي إيتاء الولد مع ترجي إيتاء الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposal takes the garden as all worldly possessions, making the better replacement include children; al-Ālūsī calls this strained.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يمكن أن يكون ترجي الولد في قوله : ( خيرا من جنتك )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group reads ghawran with ḍamma on ghayn, followed by hamza and wāw.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة ( غؤورا ) بضم الغين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers use masculine yakun because fiʾa is not feminine in sense and precedes the verb; plural yunṣarūnahu follows meaning.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان ومجاهد وابن وثاب والأعمش وطلحة وأيوب وخلف

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads takun with feminine agreement, matching fiʾa in form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة ﴿ ولم تكن له فئة ينصرونه ﴾ مراعاة للفظ فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No faction means none had power to save him, whether by preventing destruction or restoring what was destroyed identically or equivalently.
rows.anchor: والمراد من النصرة لازمها وهو القدرة عليها أي لم تكن له فئة تقدر على نصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom excludes every helper except God, but means only God has power to help; otherwise the wording would wrongly imply God rescued him.
rows.anchor: فإنه سبحانه وتعالى القادر على نصره وحده وارتكب المجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He could not defend himself by strength against God’s vengeance.
rows.anchor: في نفسه ﴿ منتصرا ﴾ ممتنعا بقوته عن انتقام الله تعالى منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Henālika means the time and place of destruction; al-wilāya can mean God’s victory alone or His support for believing allies.
rows.anchor: أي في ذلك المقام وتلك الحال التي وقع فيها الإهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī favors helping believers because the verse ends by describing the reward and outcome of God’s allies.
rows.anchor: ويعضد أن المراد نصرتهم قوله تعالى ﴿ هو خير ثوابا وخير عقبا ﴾

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī distinguishes fatḥa as help and allegiance from kasra as sovereignty and dominion.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري هي بالفتح النصرة والتولي وبالكسر السلطان والملك

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and al-Aṣmaʿī call the kasra reading erroneous based on word form; al-Ālūsī dismisses the objection.
rows.anchor: وحكى عن أبي عمرو والأصمعي أنهما قالا إن كسر الواو لحن هنا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān takes henālika to point to the afterlife, fitting the reward language and 40:16.
rows.anchor: واستظهر أبو حيان كون هنالك إشارة إلى الدار الآخرة أي في تلك الدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred syntax pauses after muntaṣiran, then begins a clause with al-wilāya as subject and lillāh as predicate, expressing exclusivity.
rows.anchor: والظاهر على جميع ذلك أن الوقف على

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj attaches henālika to muntaṣiran, meaning the man could not prevail in that state; another view points to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: والزجاج جعله متعلقا بمنتصرا أيضا إلا أنه قال ما كان منتصرا في تلك الحالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq is an adjective of the divine name in the common reading.
rows.anchor: نعت للإسم الجليل

rows.speaker: الأخوان
rows.claim: The two Kūfan readers raise al-ḥaqq as an adjective of al-wilāya; other parses make it a predicate or subject, and Ubayy’s ordering supports the adjective reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الاخوان وحميد والأعمش وابن أبي ليلى وابن مناذر

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywa and others read al-ḥaqq in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun or detached adjective.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة وزيد بن علي وعمرو بن عبيد وابن أبي عبلة وأبو السمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings ʿuqban, ʿuqbā, and ʿuqban with varied vowels all mean outcome.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأعمش وحمزة وعاصم وخلف ﴿ عقبا ﴾ بسكون القاف والتنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day is governed by an implied remember; the apparent sense is mountains uprooted and carried like clouds, as 27:88 describes.
rows.anchor: منصوب باذكر مضمرا أي اذكر يوم نقلع الجبال من أماكنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatives take the movement as parts scattered into dust or figuratively as removal; 56:5 describes pulverized mountains.
rows.anchor: وقيل نسير أجزاءها بعد أن نجعلها هباء منبثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says movement comes first, followed by mountains becoming shifting dunes and then dust; this verse depicts the first stage.
rows.anchor: والظاهر هنا أول أحوال الجبال ولا مقتضى للصرف عن الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning the mountain catastrophe warns idolaters of overwhelming events.
rows.anchor: ثم المراد بذكر ذلك تحذير المشركين ما فيه من الدواهي

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān allows yawm to modify an implied verb of saying at you have come to Us; another proposal coordinates it with at your Lord.
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو حيان وغيره كون ﴿ يوم ﴾ ظرفا للفعل المضمر عند قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordination with at your Lord makes enduring good better both with God and on Judgment Day, taking at your Lord as in His judgment.
rows.anchor: وغير واحد كونه معطوفا على ما قبله من قوله تعالى ﴿ عند ربك ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary between passive feminine or masculine, past passive, and active forms for mountain movement; passive wording conveys divine majesty.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وابن كثير وأبو عمرو والحسن وشبل وقتادة وعيسى والزهري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth is exposed as mountains, seas, buildings, and trees disappear; inhabitants emerging exposed is less apparent.
rows.anchor: أي وترى جميع جوانب الأرض ﴿ بارزة ﴾ بادية ظاهرة

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: ʿĪsā reads the seeing verb in the passive, with earth raised as its subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى وترى الأرض ببناء الفعل للمفعول ورفع الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: We gathered them means all are assembled after rising from graves; the past tense assures resurrection and judgment.
rows.anchor: أي جمعناهم إلى الموقف من كل أواب بعد أن أقمناهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the past tense shows gathering precedes mountain movement and exposure, so people witness the terrors.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري هو للدلالة على أن حشرهم قبل التسيير والبروز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other evidence places mountain movement at the first trumpet and gathering after the second, so the verse should not mean gathering before those events.
rows.anchor: فلا ينبغي حمل الآية على معنى وحشرناهم قبل ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī agrees with Abū Ḥayyān that the gathering clause is preferably circumstantial, though not required.
rows.anchor: اختيار قول أبي حيان من أولوية الحالية على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghādir means leave behind; related words for treachery and a stagnant pool preserve that sense.
rows.anchor: أي لم نترك يقال غادره وأغدره إذا تركه ومنه الغدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes God the subject of leaving none behind; Qatāda’s reading makes earth subject, echoing 84:4.
rows.anchor: وقريء يغادر بالياء التحتية على أن الضمير لله تعالى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda reads tugādir with feminine tāʾ, taking earth as subject; Abū Ḥayyān allows divine power as referent too.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة تغادر بالتاء الفوقية على أن الضمير للأرض

rows.speaker: أبان بن يزيد
rows.claim: Abān ibn Yazīd transmits from ʿĀṣim a passive form with aḥad raised as its agent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبان بن يزيد عن عاصم كذلك أو بفتح الدال مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reads naghdur with ḍamma nūn, silent ghayn, and kasra dāl.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الضحاك نغدر بضم النون وإسكان الغين وكسر الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people are brought before God’s judgment and stand in ranks or arranged in a row.
rows.anchor: ﴿ وعرضوا على ربك ﴾ أحضروا محل حكمه وقضائه

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: A report from Muʿādh says God summons servants for reckoning and orders angels to line them up on their toes.
rows.anchor: عن معاذ بن جبل أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال إن الله تعالى ينادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound report says the first and last generations gather on one plain in rows, where the caller reaches all and sight passes through them; another account gives 120 rows, 80 for this community.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث الصحيح يجمع الله تعالى الأولين والآخرين في صعيد واحد صفوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret display and ranks figuratively as troops presented before a ruler, with gathering compared to a presentation.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا عرض بالمعنى المعروف ولا اصطفاف والكلام خارج مخرج الإستعارة التمثيلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects denying actual rows: they are possible and supported by sound reports, so ṣaff need not be forced into a plural-only reading.
rows.anchor: والحق أن إنكار الاصطفاف مما لا وجه له بعد إمكانه وصحة الأخبار فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift to third person, passive voice, and address to the Prophet as your Lord heighten awe while honoring him.
rows.anchor: وفي الالتفات إلى الغيبة وبناء الفعل للمفعول مع التعرض لعنوان الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take your Lord as an allusion to divine anger and exclusion from acceptance because the unbelievers failed to recognize His lordship.
rows.anchor: وقيل في قوله تعالى ﴿ على ربك ﴾ إشارة إلى غضب الله تعالى عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: You have come to Us addresses resurrection deniers and is introduced as quoted speech, with several grammatical attachments proposed.
rows.anchor: خطاب للكفار المنكرين للبعث على إضمار القول

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī objects to attaching the day to quoted speech on syntactic grounds; al-Ālūsī says this attachment is unnatural.
rows.anchor: قال الخفاجي لأنه يصير كغلام زيد ضاربا على أن ضاربا حال من زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coming to God means arriving where false deities have no authority to benefit or harm, as in King of the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: والمراد من مجيئهم إليه تعالى مجيئهم إلى حيث لا حكم لأحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like the first creation may describe their arrival or state: barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, or stripped of possessions and supporters, as in 6:94.
rows.anchor: أو حال من الضمير المرفوع في ﴿ جئتمونا ﴾ أي كائنين كما خلقناكم أول مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes them alive as at their first creation, fitting the following rebuke about an appointment.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون المراد أحياء كخلقتكم الأولى والكلام عليه إعرابا كما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke shifts topics; mawʿidan means appointed time; jaʿala may mean make, with two objects, or create, with a circumstantial complement.
rows.anchor: وهو إضراب وانتقال من كلام إلى كلام كلاهما للتوبيخ والتقريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With jaʿala meaning make, time is its second object and appointment its first; with create, the phrase is circumstantial.
rows.anchor: والجعل إما بمعنى التصيير فالجار والمجرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placement of the book follows the presentation and is stated in the past to make the warning’s events certain; the book means records collectively.
rows.anchor: ﴿ ووضع الكتاب ﴾ عطف على عرضوا داخل تحت الأمور الهائلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Records may be given to each person’s right or left hand, placed on scales, or gathered into one book by angels; al-Ālūsī knows no report for the last view.
rows.anchor: ومن وضعه إما جعل كل كتاب في يد صاحبه اليمين أو الشمال

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Laqqānī says al-Ghazālī held that individual records are copied into one sheet, likely based on transmitted evidence.
rows.anchor: جزم الغزالي بما قيل إن صحف العباد ينسخ ما في جميعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read placing the book as metaphor for audit, but al-Ālūsī sees no need unless one denies weighing deeds.
rows.anchor: وقيل وضع الكتاب كناية عن إبراز محاسبة الخلق وسؤالهم

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads the verb actively and makes God its subject, with the book as object.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهما ﴿ ووضع الكتاب ﴾ ببناء وضع للفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Criminals, especially resurrection-denying unbelievers, fear recorded sins because they know the punishment those deeds entail.
rows.anchor: قاطبة فيدخل فيهم الكفرة المنكرون للبعث دخولا أوليا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ya waylatan personifies their ruin and calls it to come, implying ruin is their only companion and they seek it to escape punishment.
rows.anchor: يا ويلتنا ﴾ نداء لهلكتهم التي هلكوها من بين الهلكات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some propose addressing people nearby in ya waylatan, but this loses the personification’s point; mā li-hādhā al-kitāb expresses astonishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد نداء من بحضرتهم كأنه قيل يا من بحضرتنا انظروا هلكتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarsī sees no reason for the separated written lām; al-Biqāʿī says it reflects criminals pausing in distress.
rows.anchor: وزعم الطبرسي أنه لا وجه لذلك وقال البقاعي إن في رسمها كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The codex orthography is followed and its rationale may be unknown; stopping on mā or the lām is disputed, though al-Ālūsī leans toward mā.
rows.anchor: والاصح الوقف على ما لأنها كلمة مستقلة وأكثرهم لا يذكر فيها شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā yughādir means leaves nothing out; small and great wrongs are counted, a metaphor for exhaustive comprehension, either as a circumstantial or new clause.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى ﴿ لا يغادر ﴾ أي لا يترك ﴿ صغيرة ﴾ أي هنة صغيرة

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr interprets the small sin as sexual touching and the great sin as adultery.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن جبير تفسير الصغيرة بالمسيس والكبيرة بالزنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains a small sin as a mocking smile at believers and a great one as loud laughter; the reports show laughing at people is sinful.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال في الآية الصغيرة التبسم بالاستهزاء بالمؤمنين
